problem_plain: Every AI model is a long list of math steps. Before those steps can run on a real chip, someone has to translate them into the precise, tiny instructions the chip actually obeys — which wires carry which numbers, in what order, with what groupings. Today that translation is done partly by hand and partly by tools that are too rigid to spot all the shortcuts. The result: chips spend a lot of time waiting around, and wiring up a brand-new chip design can take a team of experts many months.
why_plain: A chip is fast but completely literal — it only does exactly what it is told, one tiny clock-tick at a time. The gap between 'multiply these two tables of numbers' and 'move these exact bytes to these exact wires in this exact order' is enormous. Bridging that gap well — finding the right groupings, orderings, and arrangements — is a puzzle with so many possible answers that no human team can solve it by hand at the scale modern AI demands.
approach_plain: The papers here all attack that translation gap from different angles, but share a common idea: build a richer middle-layer description of the computation — one that captures structure the final chip instructions do not — and then use that description to search for better translations automatically. Some use that middle layer to generate the chip's physical circuit directly; others use it to schedule operations more cleverly; others use a small AI model to predict which of thousands of possible translations will actually run fastest on real hardware.

groups.heading: Generating chip circuits from a description, not by hand
groups.explain: The boldest approach is to skip hand-written chip designs entirely. You describe what a computation should do in math, and a tool figures out what silicon circuit to build. This needs a description rich enough to capture how data flows, where it gets reused, and how operations are controlled — and a back-end tool that can turn that description into a real circuit blueprint. The payoff: a new AI operation can get its own custom chip in hours instead of months.

papers.name: LEGO
papers.gloss: Takes a math description of an AI operation and automatically builds a chip circuit for it, producing control logic that uses 6.5x less chip area and runs 3.2x faster than a hand-designed reference chip.

papers.name: Assassyn
papers.gloss: Write chip behavior once in a style that lists events and reactions; the tool produces both a fast simulator and a working chip blueprint — using 70% fewer lines than writing the chip blueprint by hand.

papers.name: CRUSH
papers.gloss: Lets several operations safely share one math unit in auto-generated circuits by handing out 'credits' — small tokens that stop the shared unit from being swamped with too much work at once, preventing a deadlock.

papers.name: HPVM-HDC
papers.gloss: Write one program using a style that works with very long strings of random bits (a computing method called hyperdimensional computing); the tool re-targets it to ordinary processors, graphics chips, or a custom chip without rewriting any code.

groups.heading: Simulating a chip in software before spending money to build it
groups.explain: Making a physical chip costs millions of dollars and many months, so designers test their ideas in software first. Old simulators are either very accurate but painfully slow, or fast but too rough to trust. This group of papers closes that gap, giving designers fast answers they can actually rely on.

papers.name: OmniSim
papers.gloss: Simulates auto-generated chip designs at the speed of normal software but with cycle-accurate timing — including tricky cases where operations depend on how full a data queue is — running up to 35.9x faster than the previous gold-standard simulator.

papers.name: LLMulator
papers.gloss: Uses a small fine-tuned AI model to predict how fast a chip will run a given program, spelling out timing as digit-by-digit text so it handles very different problem sizes; averages only 12.2% error on chips it has never seen.

papers.name: Concorde
papers.gloss: Predicts how fast a processor will be by combining hand-crafted pipeline math with a learned correction term — getting speed from the equations and accuracy from the neural network — so designers can search through many chip options quickly.

groups.heading: Deciding what to compute when: chunking and ordering work
groups.explain: Modern AI chips have many parallel math units, but those units only stay busy if work arrives in the right order and right-sized chunks. A 'chunk' is a piece of the computation small enough to fit in the chip's small, fast on-chip memory. Choosing the wrong chunk size or ordering is the most common reason a chip idles. The papers here develop smarter ways to pick chunk sizes and orderings so as much work as possible happens in fast on-chip memory before results are sent back to the slow main memory.

papers.name: BlockDepend
papers.gloss: Looks at which steps in a neural network depend on each other, working at chunk level rather than individual numbers — revealing hidden opportunities to merge steps and run them in parallel, giving up to 2.88x speedup over AMD's production tool.

papers.name: Mosaic
papers.gloss: Splits math operations into sub-chunks assigned at the same time to simple, medium, and powerful math units on the chip — squeezing out parallelism that sending all work to one type of unit misses.

papers.name: EDA
papers.gloss: For small chips with tight memory budgets, finds the ideal depth to keep reusing results layer by layer before sending them to slow off-chip memory — delivering 2.39x faster runs and 2.08x better energy efficiency.

papers.name: Voyager
papers.gloss: Picks step-ordering and merging strategies for graph-style networks while the program is running, because the right choice depends on the shape of each incoming graph and no single fixed plan fits them all.

papers.name: Diffuse
papers.gloss: Merges tasks and low-level compute jobs from different software libraries at runtime using a shared middle-layer description, achieving 1.86x average speedup across up to 128 graphics chips working together.

papers.name: Apophenia
papers.gloss: Automatically spots repeating patterns in a stream of parallel tasks — treating the task list like a string of text and finding repeated phrases — then saves the dependency analysis for those patterns so it never repeats that work.

groups.heading: Searching automatically for the fastest translation
groups.explain: Even after work is chunked correctly, there are thousands of valid ways to write the low-level instructions — different loop orders, memory access patterns, ways to use the chip's small set of fast registers. Trying every possibility is too slow; guessing is too inaccurate. These papers develop smarter search strategies: cheap early filters, tournament-style comparisons, and learned guessing tools that zero in on good solutions quickly.

papers.name: Pruner
papers.gloss: Speeds up the hunt for fast low-level programs by using cheap rule-based checks to eliminate most candidate arrangements first, then applying an expensive learned model only to the small set that survives.

papers.name: DarwinGame
papers.gloss: Tunes program settings on noisy shared cloud servers by running several configurations side-by-side so they all face identical interference, then ranking them in a tournament bracket — landing within 4.2% of optimal versus 40%+ error for earlier tools.

papers.name: SmoothE
papers.gloss: Turns the problem of picking the best option from a compiler's tree of choices into a smooth math curve that can be minimized by gradually adjusting numbers downhill — allowing learned cost functions too complex for simple straight-line models.

papers.name: Syno
papers.gloss: Automatically invents new AI operations by running a game-tree search over small building blocks, finding operations that run 1.37x–2.06x faster than hand-designed ones with under 1% drop in accuracy.

A position paper asking whether AI-guided systems research has hit a turning point like the 2012 moment when AI first beat humans at image recognition, surveying how AI now guides compilers, task scheduling, networking, and storage decisions.

groups.heading: One shared middle-layer description, many chip targets
groups.explain: A constant frustration in AI is that a model trained on one kind of chip has to be painfully re-coded to run on another. The fix is a standardized middle-layer description — a common language that sits between high-level Python code and low-level chip instructions. If that description is expressive enough, a single translation tool can send the same computation to graphics chips, phones, tiny embedded chips, or web browsers.

papers.name: Relax
papers.gloss: Combines high-level operation graphs, low-level loop code, and calls to outside math libraries into one middle-layer description with size labels that track unknown dimensions automatically, letting one tool target graphics chips, phones, tiny chips, and web browsers.

papers.name: PartIR
papers.gloss: Separates the question of how to split a large model across many chips from the question of how to carry out each piece, expressing each splitting strategy as a small verifiable rewrite step so strategies can be mixed, matched, and checked independently.

papers.name: StreamTensor
papers.gloss: Adds a new data type that records not just a chunk's shape but also the order a piece of compute logic streams through it — letting the tool automatically figure out how to merge steps, size buffers, and avoid deadlocks on programmable chip designs.

papers.name: Einsum Tree IR
papers.gloss: Represents a chain of number-table contractions as a tree, then optimizes how data is laid out in memory across all intermediate steps at once rather than one at a time — cutting unnecessary data movement on standard processors.

A community contest and benchmark set for the problem of splitting AI operations across multiple chips automatically, making clear how large the gap is between current tools and the best possible automatic solution.

groups.heading: Using the compiler to save energy and chip area
groups.explain: A translation tool does not just control speed — it also controls how much power the chip burns. By inspecting code before it runs, the tool can spot units that will be idle and switch them off, use narrower number formats where full precision is not needed, and avoid repeating the same calculation twice. This matters most at the extremes: tiny chips running on a battery, and large chips running around the clock in a data center.

papers.name: ReGate
papers.gloss: Adds fine-grained power switches to Google-style AI chips: detects rows and columns of the math array that hold zero and powers them off each clock tick — cutting energy 8.5%–32.8% with under 0.5% slowdown.

papers.name: BitSpec
papers.gloss: The translation tool guesses most variables need fewer bits than declared, emits narrower math, and the chip fixes the rare case where the guess was wrong at runtime — saving 9.9% average energy (up to 28.2%) on small embedded devices.

Frames reusing previously computed results on tiny microcontrollers as a problem of reordering rows and columns of a data table, uncovering far more reuse opportunities than prior work — delivering 1.03x–2.2x speedup with models that predict accuracy and run time together.

papers.name: Chassis
papers.gloss: A translation tool that jointly optimizes numerical accuracy and run speed while staying aware of exactly which math instructions the target chip supports — unifying two previously separate families of compiler thinking.

groups.heading: Translating for quantum and other unusual machines
groups.explain: Quantum computers use quantum bits that must be physically shuttled between zones — storage, calculation, readout — and each unnecessary move degrades the result. Ordinary translation tools have no model for this; quantum translation tools need entirely new scheduling ideas. Similarly, some machines solve hard puzzles by hunting for the lowest-energy state of a system, and they need special encoding to avoid wasting time on impossible answers. This group extends compiler thinking to those unusual machines.

papers.name: MUSS-TI
papers.gloss: Treats the zones of a trapped-ion quantum chip like levels of a memory hierarchy — storage zone as slow disk, operation zone as main memory, entanglement zone as fast registers — and uses a least-recently-used swap rule to cut shuttle moves by 41%–73%.

papers.name: ZAC
papers.gloss: Schedules quantum circuits on neutral-atom zone machines by keeping quantum bits in the working zone when the next operation needs them there, avoiding needless round-trips — achieving 22x better result fidelity over non-zone designs.

papers.name: PowerMove
papers.gloss: Plans quantum bit movement and gate operations together on zone-based neutral-atom machines — running 3.76x–4.78x faster, with dramatically better result quality, and compiling 216.9x faster than previous planning tools.

papers.name: Choco-Q
papers.gloss: Encodes problem constraints into a quantum search by choosing a mathematical operator that naturally commutes with (never violates) those constraints, guaranteeing every answer is valid — achieving a 235x better success rate on real IBM quantum hardware.

Inserts a small digital logic layer between an energy-minimization puzzle machine and the puzzle itself, ensuring the machine only ever explores valid answers — eliminating the penalty tricks that previously wasted 99%+ of solver time; gives 7.2x–52,000x fewer steps to a solution.

groups.heading: Strengthening the foundations that all compilers depend on
groups.explain: Behind every AI translation tool are classical building blocks — ways to assign values to a chip's small set of fast registers, ways to track data flow through a program, ways to measure software speed fairly. This group improves those foundations: smarter register assignment, easier ways to add security labels to programs, and honest critiques of flawed benchmarking habits.

papers.name: COGENT
papers.gloss: A toolchain built on the widely-used LLVM compiler that stamps variable-width security tags onto every instruction in a program, supporting any tagging policy without touching the core compiler — adding only 0.94%–5.24% run-time overhead.

Speeds up the step of assigning program variables to the chip's small set of fast registers by exploiting the branching-tree shape of how real programs flow — making a problem that is theoretically impossibly hard become fast in practice.

Shows that standard Java speed tests do not reflect real programs, because the way Java warms up its own code and manages memory creates misleading numbers — and proposes better measurement practices.

papers.name: ClosureX
papers.gloss: A compiler step that finds the smallest slice of program state that must be saved and restored between automated security-test runs, letting one running process be reused across thousands of tests without a full restart.

papers.name: Caravan
papers.gloss: Adds two new processor instructions that reorganize active slots in a wide math unit when searching nearest neighbors in 3D point clouds — achieving 5.19x speedup using only 0.032 square millimeters of extra chip area.

Introduces a bit-level algebra for describing how matrix math units work, revealing four improvements that are independent of previously known tricks — delivering 1.04x–1.56x better energy use and 1.27x–1.56x better area use on real 28-nanometer silicon.

connect: Every technique here is ultimately fighting the same bottleneck: moving data is slow and expensive, while doing math is fast and cheap. So the whole art of translation is finding arrangements of data and work that reduce how often numbers have to travel between slow main memory and the chip's fast compute units. A tool that chunks work better, merges more steps together, or generates a chip with smarter data paths is always, at root, making numbers travel shorter distances.
